citation: Tiwari, O. S., Vass, T., Singh, G. D. 'Assay: Claims That Decay With the Code. Content-Addressed Evidence Graphs for Accountable AI-Assisted Software Delivery'. arXiv:2609.36170v1 (cs.SE), 28 Sep 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36170 (HTML: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.36170v1)
source_tier: Preprint (arXiv, not peer-reviewed as far as seen)
access_status: Read via WebFetch summary of the arXiv HTML full text (not opened directly in a browser; quotes come from the fetch tool's extraction) [uncertain]

(Quotes as relayed by the fetch tool; wording not re-checked against raw HTML.) [uncertain]
date_and_recency: Submitted 28 Sep 2026 (v1). Experiments are scripted runs on five public repositories (Express, Flask, Gin, Axum, FastAPI) plus Assay itself; no data collection window stated.
key_claims: Proposes and then measures a system: each claim an AI agent makes (e.g. 'tests pass') is bound to a Merkle hash of the dependency cone of the code it concerns, so the claim is stale exactly when that code or anything it depends on changes. Staleness becomes a hash comparison, not a judgment. Adds risk-proportional evidence requirements, a bounded review protocol, and a deterministic merge gate with no model in the loop. Argues hashing only the named module is unsound; hashing the whole repo over-invalidates.
headline_figures: E1: orientation brief of 592-635 tokens is 14x to 114x cheaper than an exploration proxy (Express 28x, Flask 78x, Gin 14x, Axum 73x, FastAPI 114x). E3 (k=4 edited modules, 100 trials per point): cone-hash binding re-verifies 16.6% (Express), 66.7% (Flask), 81.9% (Gin), 66.3% (Axum), 7.9% (FastAPI), 87.4% (Assay itself); self-hash binding misses stale claims 27.8%, 45.7%, 29.3%, 67.6%, 22.7%, 7.4% respectively; repo-hash re-verifies 100% everywhere. E4: 12 scripted scenarios on a 12-file Python project, 3 honest paths pass, 9 adversarial behaviours all fail at the gate. E5: median single-module blast radius 0.5% (FastAPI), 1.1% (Axum); Axum 90th percentile 91.1%. The paper has internal inconsistencies between abstract ranges and Table III.
sample_unit_and_population: Five public open-source repositories (Express, Flask, Gin, Axum, FastAPI) plus Assay's own code, and one 12-file synthetic Python project for the gate test. Unit is module / edit simulation; no human participants, no LLM agents run.
observed_vs_stated: Observed in scripted simulation (simulated edits and scripted adversary), not behaviour of real agents or developers. The effect on LLM agent performance is not measured.
what_makes_trust_justified: Evidence bound to content hashes of the code cone, so a passing test result is only honoured while the code it covered is unchanged; stale claims must be re-attested. Risk-proportional evidence obligations (L0-L3), separation of doer and reviewer, signed attestations, and a model-free merge gate.
what_it_costs: Index build time (FastAPI cold 508 ms, one-edit 106 ms, no-change 93 ms), re-verification of claims inside the blast radius (up to 87% of claims for k=4 edits in some repos), and review effort under the protocol. Human cost not measured.
failure_mode_class: False report / stale evidence: an agent's 'tests pass' or similar claim that no longer holds after later code changes; also an adversarial or sloppy doer gaming the gate.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. The control proposed is cone-hash binding plus gate that rejects stale, unsigned or implausible claims.
limitations_stated: Sec. VIII: regex-based import extraction is the largest source of unsoundness; directory-level modules are coarse and inflate radii; the gate checks plausibility, not evidence sufficiency; signing key placement outside agent reach is described, not enforced; extensions beyond tests (docs, lockfiles, infrastructure) are proposed, not evaluated; model-in-the-loop evaluation designed but not run. Sec. VI-G: import graphs under-approximate dependencies (dynamic imports, reflection, generated code); E4 attacks designed by the same authors; one tokenizer; exploration proxy stands in for agent behaviour.
counter_evidence: Related preprint 'Impact Is Not Invalidation: Ask About the Claim, Not the Diff' (arXiv 2609.25130) suggests dependency impact does not equal invalidation, which would cut against hash-based over-invalidation; only its title/reference list was seen [uncertain]. Within the paper, cone binding can still re-verify a large share of claims (up to 87%), and the 90th-percentile blast radius is large (Axum 91.1%), so churn may be high.
verification_status: Paper content checked only through a fetch-tool summary of the arXiv HTML, not read in full by me. Numbers and quotes [uncertain] until spot-checked against the page. Related-work claim about 2609.25130 unverified [uncertain].
usable_claim: A 2026 preprint proposes binding each agent claim (such as 'tests pass') to a hash of the code it depends on, so the claim is treated as stale as soon as that code changes, and reports simulated experiments on five open-source repositories. It is a design plus scripted simulation, not evidence that this improves outcomes with real agents.
do_not_use: Do not cite the 14x to 114x token saving, re-verification percentages or 'sound and minimal' as proof the approach works in practice; they are simulations by the tool's authors with no LLM agents or humans. Do not say it was tested on real agent output. Do not use the abstract's ranges (inconsistent with Table III).
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays [uncertain]. Idea of evidence going stale after code changes is likely complementary rather than duplicate.
